title: Giving the River Rib room to breathe: restoring a Hertfordshire chalk stream

content.content: Some of England's most special rivers flow almost unnoticed through our countryside. Chalk streams are among the rarest freshwater habitats on Earth, with around 85% of the world's 280 chalk streams found in England.

These rivers are renowned for their crystal-clear waters, rich wildlife and cultural heritage. Yet many have been heavily modified over generations, leaving them disconnected from their natural processes and struggling to support healthy ecosystems.

This summer, we worked in partnership with the Wild Trout Trust, Affinity Water and local landowner Jeffrey Pearman to undertake a major restoration project on a one-kilometre stretch of the River Rib at Latchford, near Standon in Hertfordshire, to help return a section of this precious chalk stream to a more natural condition.
A river shaped by the past
Like many rivers across England, this stretch of the River Rib has been altered by decades of dredging, straightening and neighbouring agricultural land use.

Over time, these changes deepened the river, removed important gravel habitats and disconnected the channel from its floodplain. Natural processes that once maintained a healthy and diverse river environment were lost, contributing to the ‘moderate’ ecological condition of the waterbody under the 2025 Water Framework Directive classification.
Thinking bigger
What made this project particularly exciting was the opportunity to think beyond the existing river channel.

The landowner, Jeffrey Pearman, was willing to dedicate additional land to the project, allowing us to create a more ambitious restoration than would otherwise have been possible. Rather than simply modifying the existing channel, the team was able to create approximately 300 metres of ‘re-wiggled’ river channel and reconnect the river to its wider floodplain.
This approach gives the river more space to move through the landscape naturally, helping it respond to both high and low flow conditions while creating valuable habitat for wildlife.

The approach reflects the principles of the Chalk Stream Restoration Strategy, which promotes restoring natural river processes and reconnecting rivers with their floodplains to improve the long-term health and resilience of chalk stream catchments.
Rob Mungovan, Project Manager at the Wild Trout Trust, said:

"Chalk streams are incredibly special habitats, and projects like this are about giving rivers the space and natural features they need to function properly. Jeff's ambition as a landowner allowed us to push what was possible here. Rather than being constrained by the existing channel, we were able to create something much more ambitious for the River Rib and the wildlife that depends on it."
Restoring natural processes
The restoration works were delivered by Aquamaintain and overseen by the Wild Trout Trust, with support from the Environment Agency and Affinity Water.
The project included:

An unexpected but beneficial aspect of the project was the discovery of substantial quantities of gravel during excavation works. Some of this material was processed and reused on site, helping recreate the riverbed conditions required by native chalk stream species.
Benefits for wildlife
Healthy chalk streams support an extraordinary range of plants and animals.

The restoration will improve habitat for fish species including brown trout, while also benefiting aquatic plants, invertebrates and a wide variety of wetland wildlife. The creation of new wetland habitats and improved floodplain connectivity is expected to provide new opportunities for species such as water voles, otters, wading birds and insects.
By restoring natural river processes, we are not only improving conditions within the channel itself but helping to recover ecological connections across the wider landscape.
Partnership in action
Projects of this scale simply cannot happen without strong partnerships.

The Environment Agency provided funding through the Chalk Partnership Fund and Water Environment Improvement Fund. The Wild Trout Trust led on project development and delivery, while Affinity Water provided support and funding through its ambitious River Restoration programme as part of its wider environmental commitments to protect chalk stream catchments, enhance biodiversity and improve water quality, helping to leave the environment in a measurably improved state. The success of the project also relied on the enthusiasm and commitment of the landowner, who not only made his land available for the restoration works but also provided practical support to Aquamaintain throughout project delivery.
The project demonstrates what can be achieved when organisations bring together their expertise, resources and shared commitment to improving the environment.
George Horne, Senior River Restoration Project Manager at Affinity Water, said:

"This project shows what can be achieved when landowners, environmental organisations and water companies bring their different expertise together around a shared ambition for our chalk streams. Creating more space for the River Rib and restoring the features it would naturally have helps create a healthier environment for wildlife and forms part of the wider work needed to protect these precious habitats for the future."
Looking ahead
While construction has now been completed, the story of the River Rib restoration is only just beginning.

Extensive seeding and tree planting is planned, which will help transform the currently exposed riverbanks, with wetter weather helping vegetation to establish and stabilise the banks alongside ongoing monitoring to understand how the river responds over time. The site will also provide valuable lessons for future chalk stream restoration projects across Hertfordshire and beyond.

Our ambition is that the River Rib becomes an example of how working with natural processes can help restore England's globally rare chalk streams, improve resilience to climate change and create thriving environments for people and wildlife. In doing so, the project supports the Environment Agency's EA2030 ambitions for healthy air, land and water supporting nature's recovery, and for creating a nation that is more resilient to climate change.
By giving the river room to breathe once again, we are helping to secure a healthier future for this special ecosystem.

title: Who’s eligible for the 2026 COVID-19 vaccine, or ‘Autumn Booster’?

content.content: When autumn comes, protection from any earlier COVID-19 vaccination you may have had will be starting to wane. For those who are more likely to become seriously ill from COVID-19, the NHS offers a free vaccine in the autumn, previously known as the 'Autumn Booster'.

Current vaccines provide good protection against severe disease and hospitalisation. UKHSA surveillance data relating to last autumn's programme shows that vaccine effectiveness was 47% for the 3 months following vaccination.

Vaccination continues to help protect against severe illness, hospitalisations and deaths arising from COVID-19. NHS England data suggests that between October 2025 and January 2026 around 16,000 people were admitted to hospital with the virus.
Eligible groups for autumn 2026

Ministers have accepted the advice of the Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation (JCVI) for the autumn 2026 COVID-19 vaccination programme, which focuses on vaccinating those at highest risk of serious disease.
For autumn 2026, COVID-19 vaccination is offered to:
The eligibility is the same across the 4 nations of the UK (England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland).

The vaccine should usually be offered no earlier than around 6 months after the last vaccine dose. If you are eligible, you can get protection from an autumn COVID-19 vaccination even if you have not taken up a COVID-19 vaccine offer in the past.
Eligibility for the immunosuppressed

We understand that having a weakened immune system (immunosuppression) is a lot less straightforward than the other criteria. Looking online can cause even more confusion, as people might see themselves (and be considered by others) as immunosuppressed but might not fit the immunosuppression criteria for vaccination.

So, what are the immunosuppression criteria? Eligibility is outlined in the COVID-19 Green Book chapter, a document published by UKHSA specifically for public health professionals. It can be a complicated document for non-experts, so we've listed some of the groups here:
While this list summarises some major groups, it does not cover everything. Please talk to your healthcare professional if you are unsure.
How to access the COVID-19 autumn vaccination
COVID-19 spreads more easily in winter because we spend more time indoors with others.

Booking for the COVID-19 vaccination is now open. Visit the NHS website and choose a date and time from 1 October. If you are eligible, having your COVID-19 vaccination this autumn will give you protection from serious COVID illness over winter.

title: Making graph databases more accessible with AI

content.content: The bottleneck between questions and answers

Graph databases are designed to store and analyse relationships between connected pieces of data. Analysts working with graph databases often know exactly what question they want answered, but not how to write the query needed to get that answer. A seemingly simple question such as "How does this product move through Company X's supply chain?" can require a complex Cypher query involving multiple connected suppliers, products and routes.

This challenge was raised to us by colleagues in the Global Supply Chains Intelligence Programme (GSCIP). This is a platform that brings together large-scale data to help government understand global supply chains.

While GSCIP analysts need quick access to answers from graph data, many do not use Cypher day-to-day. As a result, data scientists often spend significant time translating business questions into database queries. This can create a bottleneck between the people who understand the problem and the people who understand the database.

To explore whether AI could help bridge this gap, we built a proof of concept (PoC) that translates plain English into graph database queries. Our goal was simple: find out if this approach is feasible and understand the trade-offs involved. This would help to inform us about how AI could reduce pressure on specialist teams, and what guardrails would be needed in a live environment.
The experiment
Our lightweight proof of concept was designed for rapid experimentation.

At a high level, the system allows a user to ask a question in plain English, such as "Which organisations are connected to this project?" and automatically converts that question into a database query. The system then retrieves the relevant information from a graph database and returns the results.

To keep the design flexible, we exposed the capability through a simple interface that could be integrated with other tools and tested against a range of example questions. This allowed us to focus on the core challenge: reliably translating natural language into queries that can navigate complex relationships in graph data.

For readers interested in the technical implementation, the solution was built using a graph database and a text-to-query component that generates Cypher queries from natural language, as shown in Figure 1.
Synthetic data supporting AI development and testing
To support development and testing, we built a synthetic data generator capable of producing graph data matching the data structure and size we would expect in a real environment.
This allowed us to generate realistic test data and quickly load it into the platform through an API, without exceeding the capacity of our local systems.
Using synthetic data gave us more flexibility in the testing process and minimised the need to process real data.
How can we be sure it works?

Before releasing the tool to analysts, we needed a robust way to assess the reliability of its generated queries. We used DeepEval, which is an evaluation framework for Large Language Models (LLMs), to evaluate query quality and performance.

We also recognised the limitations of using LLMs to evaluate LLMs (LLM-as-a-judge), as is done with DeepEval. To mitigate this, we complemented automated evaluation with targeted human reviews, helping us better understand failure modes and measure true accuracy.
What we learned: a correct query is not always the right query

While the experiment was not intended to benchmark production-level accuracy, it demonstrated that natural language questions could be translated into executable graph queries across a range of test scenarios. This gave us confidence that the approach was feasible.

One of the most important findings was that generating syntactically valid, runnable queries is not the hardest problem. The greater challenge is ensuring that each query genuinely reflects the user's intent. As a result, the same question can sometimes produce different answers depending on how that intent is interpreted.

This has important implications for anyone looking to build on or replicate this work: evaluation cannot focus solely on query correctness but must also assess whether the generated query captures the intended meaning of the original request. This increases the need for careful testing.
A spectrum of approaches
One of the key questions for this experiment was understanding what kind of approach is even feasible. In practice, translating natural language into graph queries sits on a spectrum:

The experiment highlighted a trade-off between flexibility and consistency. Fully generative approaches are more flexible, but produce less consistent results. Deterministic approaches offer greater reliability, but narrower coverage. Our testing suggested that a hybrid approach may offer the most practical balance between the two. A deterministic query bank can handle common, well-understood questions, while LLM generation is reserved for unusual or more complex questions. This shifts effort away from continuous runtime validation toward upfront verification of trusted query patterns.
Benefits of our work

This work did more than test whether the technology could work. It gave us a clearer understanding of how we could make graph data more accessible to analysts. It also helped us test similar AI approaches more safely in the future.
Understanding the feasibility of the idea

Our experiment demonstrated that natural language querying of graph data using LLMs is technically feasible, while also identifying important practical challenges around consistency, evaluation, and intent matching.

Understanding these limitations early helps reduce risk and provides a clearer foundation for future development. Building on this foundation could make complex graph data easier to interrogate for analysts and reduce repetitive query-writing requests for data scientists.
Building our own capability

The project also built reusable capability. We now have in-house tools and processes to generate synthetic datasets and evaluate LLM performance across both graph and non-graph use cases, simply by providing a schema and relevant inputs.

This has already accelerated experimentation across our AI teams. It will make future AI projects at BIST faster and cheaper to test before deciding whether to scale them. The lessons and evaluation methods developed through this work are also relevant across the public sector, where organisations face similar challenges in testing AI systems safely, reliably, and cost-effectively. Get in touch if you'd like to talk further about this.
What's next

The next step is understanding what it would take to move forward to a production-ready capability, if the approach proves reliable enough. This includes validating performance at scale, integrating with real environments and implementing appropriate guardrails and security controls.

We are also exploring ways to use AI to generate more realistic synthetic data. Rather than creating data that only follows the required structure, the aim is to generate data that better reflects real-world relationships and patterns. Over time, we hope this will make synthetic datasets more useful for testing and evaluating new AI applications.

Explainability is another focus area. We want to enable users not just to query data in plain English, but to receive results that are clearly explained and visualised. This would make graph data far more accessible to non-technical users.

Looking further ahead, there is potential to automate more parts of the experimentation process. For example, agents could support synthetic data generation, proof-of-concept creation, evaluation and quality assurance. This could reduce the time and effort required to evaluate new ideas. It could allow teams to test more concepts and focus their attention on higher-value review and decision-making activities. However, any such approach would require robust guardrails and multiple human checkpoints to ensure reliability and trust. These kinds of approaches benefit from collaboration between government and industry delivery partners, combining technical expertise with experience from a range of sectors.
Conclusion

This experiment showed that using AI to query graph databases in plain English is technically feasible. It has the potential to make complex network data more accessible to a wider range of users. However, the key lesson is that generating a valid query is not enough. The greater challenge is ensuring that the query accurately reflects the user's intent and consistently returns the answer they are actually looking for.

For data scientists, analysts and Digital and Data leaders considering similar approaches, this means placing as much emphasis on evaluation, governance and human review as on the AI technology itself. Success should be measured not only by whether a query runs, but by whether it produces trusted and meaningful results.

We would like to hear from others exploring AI-assisted querying, synthetic data generation or AI evaluation. How are you assessing whether AI-generated outputs reflect user intent? Where have you found human oversight remains essential?

description: What if analysts could query graph databases using plain English? This experiment tested AI-assisted querying, uncovering practical benefits, challenges and considerations for future adoption across government.

title: What is an accelerator?
authors: Anna Goss, Deputy Director - Test, Learn and Grow, Public Sector Reform, Cabinet Office

content.content: In Autumn 2025 we started our accelerator projects: small, multidisciplinary teams working alongside places to design, test and scale solutions to complex public service challenges.

Rather than designing a solution centrally and rolling it out, an accelerator brings together people from central and local government to work side by side on a shared challenge. It will include people with a variety of skills such as service design, data, product, policy, analysis and delivery. This way of working means that solutions are designed for and specific to the needs of the communities we’re serving.

The accelerators are also trying to prove that test and learn is a legitimate and effective way of developing public policy close to the people we're serving. We are continuously evaluating, learning and adapting as we go. What we learn during the course of the accelerators directly shapes how we think about public service reform more broadly.

There's no fixed length to an accelerator: the timeline depends on the nature of the challenge and what the team and place partner learn along the way. What's consistent across every accelerator is the approach.
Starting with people, not assumptions

Every accelerator begins the same way: by listening, understanding and building relationships with places and our partners. Before anyone designs a solution, teams spend time understanding the problem from the perspective of the people living with it, whether that's residents, frontline practitioners, schools, the voluntary sector or local delivery partners. In most cases this means spending time in places to understand how communities experience their daily lives such as travelling to work or support services. It could also mean interviews with service users where they outline any issues they are facing, or sitting with local teams to understand how services currently work and where they fall short.
This stage matters because it's easy to wrongly assume you know what the problem is. Test and learn only works if you're honest about what you don't yet know.
Designing together

Once a team has a clearer picture of the problem, the next step is participatory design: bringing local partners, delivery staff, and often service users themselves into the room to collaborate and generate ideas together. The people who understand the local context and deliver services day to day help shape what gets tested. This is central to how we work.

Rather than committing to a large-scale rollout, accelerators test the riskiest assumptions first on a small scale. This might mean testing whether a particular group can be identified and reached before testing whether an intervention changes behaviour, or trying an idea with a handful of people before expanding it.

Starting small lowers risk. It means that if an assumption turns out to be wrong, the team finds out quickly and cheaply, rather than after investing months of effort and funding into something that doesn't work. It also means we can adapt fast when we learn something unexpected, rather than being locked into a plan that no longer fits the evidence.
Learning, always

We treat learning as continuous, not as a single phase with an endpoint. Every test, whether it succeeds or fails to produce the expected result, generates evidence that shapes what happens next. Teams regularly review findings, adjust their approach, and sometimes go back to first principles when something doesn't work as expected.

This means being honest about what doesn't go to plan. If a test doesn't produce the results we hoped for, that's not a failure of the programme, it's exactly how the model is supposed to work. We'd rather learn that something doesn't work on a small scale, quickly, than find out after a much larger rollout.

While each accelerator is rooted in a specific place, the aim is never just local improvement. Every accelerator is designed to generate insight that can inform national policy and practice and highlight wider, systemic barriers. This could include data-sharing arrangements, funding structures, or ways of working, that get in the way of good public service delivery everywhere.
That's why in Test, Learn, Grow we work hard to build feedback loops with central government departments, feeding what they learn locally back into national policy development and guidance.
Working as partners, not hierarchies

Underpinning all of this is a particular way of working. Accelerator teams don't sit above local partners directing activity, they work alongside them, as equals with different roles and expertise. Ideas, feedback and decisions flow in all directions.

This is important because accelerators are tackling challenges that are usually too complex for any single organisation or level of government to solve alone. Progress depends on genuine partnership between national and local government, alongside the wider ecosystem of place, which includes community organisations and citizens.
Nicola Bailey, Early Years and Family Hubs Service Lead in Manchester said:

“What Test, Learn and Grow does is create space for people to think differently and by turning up today the government is showing the level of commitment they’ve got to changing the outcomes for children and families and for us as a city..
“I always feel that my contribution is valued.”
What's next

Each of our accelerators is at a different stage and each is dealing with a genuinely difficult public service challenge. Over the coming months we'll share more from each place: what we're testing, what's working, and what isn't. We'll also introduce you to some of the people delivering this work on the ground in the places themselves.
If you want to follow along, you can subscribe for email notifications using the sign-up link, or join the Test, Learn and Grow community on LinkedIn.

description: In Autumn 2025 we started our accelerator projects: small, multidisciplinary teams working alongside places to design, test and scale solutions to complex public service challenges. This blog takes you through what an accelerator is, who is involved, the ways of working that underpin them, and what they aim to achieve.

title: Every sighting matters! Why your report matters in the fight against the yellow-legged hornet

content.content: The United Kingdom's (UK) response to the invasive yellow-legged hornet relies on more than specialist inspectors and technology, it relies on the public.

Recent scientific modelling undertaken by researchers working with APHA has highlighted the vital role that citizen science plays in slowing the spread of yellow-legged hornets. The findings suggest that prompt public reporting of sightings and nests is one of the most important factors determining whether incursions can be successfully located and eradicated before populations become established.
Every report makes a difference

Yellow-legged hornets can spread rapidly if nests remain undetected. The research indicates that the success of eradication efforts depends on finding and destroying nests before hornet numbers increase beyond the capacity of response teams to investigate and track them.
The model identified several key risks:
Reaching the eradication tipping point

APHA's National Bee Unit works hard to investigate credible sightings and locate nests. However, if growing hornet numbers result in more nests than can be traced and destroyed, the likelihood of successful eradication decreases significantly. Early reporting remains critical.
Protecting pollinators

Yellow-legged hornets are effective predators of insects, including pollinators. European studies have suggested that impacts can be significant in areas where the species becomes established, posing risks to biodiversity, pollination and beekeeping.
Evidence that control is possible

Genetic analysis of nests destroyed in England indicates that many incursions appear to result from repeated introductions rather than large established populations. This means that rapid detection, tracking and nest destruction can still be highly effective in preventing long-term establishment.
The public is part of the solution
The UK's response has benefited enormously from members of the public, beekeepers and nature enthusiasts who have taken the time to learn how to recognise and report yellow-legged hornets.
Every photograph submitted and every credible sighting reported helps to build a clearer picture of hornet activity and supports inspectors in locating nests.
In short: if people stop reporting, our chances of finding nests and protecting UK pollinators fall dramatically.
What you can do
If you think you have seen a yellow-legged hornet:
Take a photograph if it is safe to do so.
Record the location.
Report the sighting using the Asian Hornet Watch App or the UKCEH online reporting form.
Do not attempt to destroy a nest yourself.
Even if you are unsure, submitting a report allows specialists to assess the evidence and determine whether further investigation is needed.

When people look and report, we find hornets! The modelling highlights just how important public reporting is to the UK's response. In areas where yellow-legged hornets are most frequently detected, such as Kent and around Plymouth, high levels of vigilance and reporting must be maintained to ensure new incursions are identified quickly. However, the research also points to another challenge: regions with fewer people, including parts of Wales, may be at greater risk of hornet populations becoming established unnoticed. Whilst these areas provide suitable habitat for yellow-legged hornets, lower numbers of people can mean fewer sightings are reported, reducing the chances of early detection. Every report matters. Whether you live in a known hotspot or a rural area, taking a photograph and reporting a suspected sighting could provide the crucial clue that helps APHA locate and destroy a nest before it has the opportunity to spread.

Yellow-legged Hornet Week is an opportunity to recognise the contribution made by thousands of people across England and Wales who have reported sightings, raised awareness and supported surveillance efforts.
The message is simple: See it - Snap it - Send it

By remaining vigilant and reporting suspected sightings, the public continues to play a crucial role in protecting pollinators, supporting beekeeping and helping to prevent the establishment of this invasive species in the UK.

title: Copilot and me: What’s made a difference

content.content: Since 2023, Defra has been running targeted trials and rollouts of Microsoft Copilot – a personal AI assistant integrated within Microsoft apps. These pilots highlighted the meaningful ways AI can benefit colleagues who are neurodivergent and/or have a disability or other accessibility need. As such, Defra made full licences available as a reasonable adjustment earlier this year, and I was issued with one.
As a team leader and strategic technical officer, I manage and support people while leading the team operationally to deliver our priorities effectively.

I oversee complex compliance and enforcement work and help shape consistent technical approaches across the team. My role combines day-to-day people leadership with strategic advice, improvement work and collaboration with others to protect people and the environment.
Stepping into the unknown

When I was given access to Copilot, I wasn't quite sure what to expect. Like many people, I thought it would be useful for drafting documents and answering questions, but I quickly realised it could be much more than that.

As someone with dyslexia, I have always found that my brain works quickly. I often know what I want to say and have lots of ideas but getting those thoughts onto paper in a clear and structured way can take time and effort. Reading large amounts of text, checking spelling and grammar, and formatting documents can all add to the processing time needed to complete a task.

Over the years I've used a range of support tools to help with different aspects of my work. What surprised me about Copilot is that it feels like many of those tools have been brought together in one place.
Focusing on the message

I use Copilot every day across Outlook, Teams and Word. It helps me review and improve written work, summarise lengthy emails and documents, check spelling and grammar, and organise information into a format that is easier to work with. Rather than spending lots of time focusing on the mechanics of writing, I can focus on the message I want to get across.

The biggest difference for me is that Copilot helps me work at the pace my brain naturally works. The ideas, knowledge and creativity are still mine, but Copilot helps me turn them into something clear and accessible much more quickly. It feels less like a replacement for my skills and more like a tool that enhances them.
Giving me confidence to be creative

It has also helped me feel more confident. Instead of worrying about whether I've missed a spelling mistake or whether a document flows properly, I can spend more time focusing on the quality of my work and the outcomes I'm trying to achieve.

One feature I particularly enjoy is the ability to be digitally creative. Developing ideas, drafting communications and exploring different ways of presenting information can often take time. Copilot helps me get those ideas out of my head and into a format that I can refine and build on. It allows me to be more productive without losing my own voice.

For me, Copilot is an assistive technology as much as it is an AI tool. It helps remove some of the barriers that dyslexia can create and gives me more time to focus on the things I do best. The result is that I spend less time processing text and more time contributing, creating and adding value.
Making Copilot work with you, not for you

If I could give one piece of advice to anyone starting out with Copilot, it would be to use it as a partner rather than expecting it to do the work for you. The more you use it to support your own strengths, the more value you'll get from it.
In many ways, Copilot has helped me unlock more of my potential at work, and that's probably the biggest difference it has made.

Most notably, I spend less time battling with the mechanics of reading and writing and more time using my skills, experience and creativity. It has helped me reach my potential in ways that feel both practical and empowering.
More information
Zoe Wilson is an enforcement senior team leader in the Environment Agency’s reservoir regulation team.

If you're interested in finding out more about what we do in Defra Digital Data Technology and Security check out our LinkedIn page for all the latest news, stories and job openings. While you're there, why not give us a follow?

title: Rigged bids, real costs - the case for tackling bid rigging in public procurement

content.content: In 2023, the CMA fined 10 construction firms £60 million for colluding to rig the bidding processes for demolition and asbestos removal contracts worth £150 million. The evidence in the case included emails, text messages and handwritten notes - even a notebook with names of contractors next to compensation figures which firms owed one another for rigging bids in their favour.

This was a case of brazen illegality, targeting sites which included the Met Police training college and Oxford University. But the case also illustrates a wider point: too often, the real victims of bid rigging are taxpayers, who could be paying up to 20% or more (according to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, OECD) for vital public services, infrastructure and national security. Desperately needed money, which goes directly from stretched departmental budgets into the pockets of colluding firms.

Public procurement spend in the UK is in the region of £400 billion per year. No precise estimate of the impact of bid rigging is possible – the activity, after all, happens in secret and evidence suggests detected cases could be the tip of the iceberg. But the CMA believes the cost to the taxpayer might be between £1 billion and £3.5 billion.

The reality is that features like the nature and frequency of tenders (amongst others) make public sector procurement a prime target for bid rigging. In fact, over half all the bid rigging cases the CMA has investigated have involved public sector tenders. Figures from international authorities show the UK is by no means an outlier.

Nor is the cost purely financial. Evidence also points to reduced quality and innovation, sometimes with very real human consequences - from increases in road traffic accidents due to substandard infrastructure, to increased hospital mortality due to depleted budgets for essential medicines.

Historically, detection has been challenging – with such high rewards, and serious consequences if caught, colluding firms have strong incentives to hide their activity. Whistleblowing plays an important role, but caches of incriminating text messages and emails don’t just fall into the laps of competition authorities every day.

The good news is that a step change in detection is now possible, driven by advanced data science and AI. Around the world, governments and competition authorities (Spain, Portugal, Brazil, Korea, to name a few), are using data screening tools to hunt for suspicious patterns at scale. It is working. But it relies on one critical factor: access to the right data, at scale - including, crucially, losing tender bids.

The CMA has invested substantially in this area over recent years, combining deep cartel enforcement expertise with advanced data science. The product of that investment is BRIT - our Bid Rigging Intelligence Tool, which offers cutting edge capabilities to analyse data at scale across the public sector to find suspicious patterns.

BRIT can’t reach its true potential until it has access to the data needed for systematic screening at scale. Unlike in many countries, this data is not routinely collected or available in machine readable format here. We are running pilots with public bodies, including the Departments for Education, Work and Pensions and Justice. These pilots are already generating promising leads. Thus far, however, there has not been a cross-government commitment to create an accessible, large scale data set - in contrast to the experience in many other jurisdictions internationally.

Today, I am in Parliament presenting CMA recommendations to reform public procurement, of which our proposals on bid rigging form a key part. Most importantly, we are calling on government to unlock bid rigging capability at scale through a more coordinated approach to data. This would bring the UK in line with international counterparts and potentially save billions of pounds of taxpayer’s money.

title: Why beauty still matters: reflections on a career spent fighting for our finest landscapes

content.content: By Marian Spain, Chief Executive, Natural England

As she nears the end of her career at Natural England, Chief Executive Marian Spain reflects on 40 years working with Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty, from their early days as planning tools to their evolution into today's thriving National Landscapes. She traces the milestones that shaped this journey, and marks the moment with the submission of formal orders to extend the Surrey Hills AONB and create a new National Landscape in the Yorkshire Wolds.

40 years ago, when I started my nature conservation career working across the east and south of England, National Parks weren't really part of my world so the Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty, or AONBs, became my natural allies.

Historically, AONBs were almost entirely about planning. Their job was to stop development happening in the wrong places, but there was very little positive, active management of the countryside and they were often seen as the poorer relation to National Parks. Less funding, less action, less influence.

I am very proud therefore that I at one point held a job called "Head of Finest Countryside" (even though plenty of people pointed out, quite fairly, that this was also the name of a supermarket's premium food range!). But behind the slightly awkward title was a serious responsibility: improving the management of every AONB and National Park in the country. That was the moment when we started to see local authorities begin to invest in teams to look after AONBs, and to see them not just as places to protect from harm, but as places for nature to recover and for people to enjoy.

That shift fed into the Countryside and Rights of Way Act 2000, which gave AONBs statutory management plans for the first time, and created the ability to establish Conservation Boards. It was a small but important change in the law that gave these nationally significant landscapes a firmer footing.

I also worked on the designations of the New Forest and South Downs as National Parks. Those projects sparked long debates about whether other AONBs needed to be "upgraded" to fulfil their potential too. Whatever the answer, the conversation itself pushed everyone to try harder.

It was always clear to me that AONBs were never second best. The legislation is unambiguous: it sets exactly the same standard of natural beauty for an AONB as for a National Park.  The bodies that look after AONBs were not bound by formal planning and other duties and governance as National Park Authorities are, nor did they have the same resources, so they could (and often had to be) entrepreneurial and innovative and build partnerships that reached wide and far. Necessity became a strength.

Then came the Landscapes Review chaired by Julian Glover, which asked hard questions about whether our system of protected landscapes was fit for the 21st century. Natural England contributed evidence throughout, and its recommendations have shaped much of what has followed.

Today, we have AONBs rebranded as National Landscapes, and a National Landscapes Association that champions them and pushes all of them towards the highest standards. We have the Protected Landscapes Partnership that brings National Trails, National Landscapes and National Parks together as one family. That means they work collectively on projects that transcend their boundaries, such as the “Big Chalk” project and Coastal Wildbelt.

That new vigour and ambition and collective effort is also being recognised through new designations: National Landscapes, as they have evolved to be, are as relevant today as they were the concept was first established in law in 1949.

When I joined Natural England in 2018, one of my first jobs was to sign the Order designating an extension to the Suffolk Coast and Heaths AONB. It feels fitting that, as I approach the end of my role as CEO here and the last stage of my 40-year career in nature, that I have last week with the NE Chair signed the Orders that contribute towards the potential creation/extension of two more National Landscapes. Today (7 September 2026) marks the submission of the formal orders to the Secretary of State seeking to extend Surrey Hills AONB and seeking a brand new AONB in the Yorkshire Wolds.

Whilst those landscapes are not designated unless or until the SoS confirms the decision, today, the whole family of National Landscapes are delivering on the ground in ways that would have seemed unimaginable when I started out.

Take Heathland Connections in the Surrey Hills, restoring and reconnecting fragmented heathland habitats so that wildlife can move and thrive across a landscape rather than being confined to isolated pockets. Or the Farming in Protected Landscapes scheme, which has given farmers right across our National Landscapes practical support and funding to farm sustainably, proving that food production and nature recovery can go hand in hand.

And then there's the simple, profound fact that millions of people visit these landscapes - including the Yorkshire Wolds which is home to the Yorkshire Wolds National Trail - every year for their health and wellbeing, finding space to breathe, to walk, to think. National Landscapes are places that are valued and protected not just for their beauty but are managed and promoted for everything they give us.
A landscape's work is never finished

Whatever comes next for our landscapes, I know they are in good hands. The people who care for them, who campaign for them, and who simply walk through them and are quietly changed by what they see, will make sure of that. It has been the privilege of my working life to stand alongside them.
Further information on the Yorkshire Wolds project is available at Yorkshire Wolds Designation Project
Further information on the Surrey Hills project is available at Surrey Hills National Landscape (AONB) Variation Project Second Consultation - Defra - Citizen Space

title: Why we're discussing meat inspection charges at our next Board meeting

content.content: Cymraeg

Our job at the Food Standards Agency (FSA) is to make sure food is safe and authentic. In the meat sector, that means carrying out robust inspections in abattoirs and meat processing businesses. This work protects the health of people and animals, supports animal welfare, and helps to maintain confidence in British meat.

At our next FSA Board meeting, we will be discussing the future of financial support for these inspections and considering recommendations following a significant programme of engagement with industry and a recent public consultation.
Over the past two years, we have worked extensively with businesses, trade bodies and other stakeholders to consider how taxpayer-funded discounts to meat inspection charges should operate in future.

The current arrangements provide financial support to businesses across the sector, but the evidence gathered through consultation suggests support should be more closely targeted at smaller abattoirs, where regulatory costs can be a greater burden.
Smaller abattoirs often play an important role in rural economies, supporting local food production and providing services that are valued by farmers, producers and consumers.

The proposals that the FSA Board will discuss are intended to ensure that taxpayers’ money is used in a way that delivers these wider benefits to the food system and the economy, while continuing to support food safety and consumer confidence. You can read more on these proposals in the Board paper.

Inspection charges remain a concern  for many businesses, and we understand the pressure they're under from increasing costs. That's why it's important that decisions about future support are informed by evidence, on-going consultation with the industry, and a clear understanding of the wider impact on the sector.

As a transparent regulator, we want those with an interest in this issue to have the opportunity to hear the Board's discussion first hand. Our Board meetings are held in public and you’re welcome to attend in person or join remotely, so you can follow the discussion and hear the Board's considerations directly.

The meeting is on Wednesday 16 September in Swansea. The agenda also includes a range of other important food issues including the future of food regulation, our annual science update, and the regulation of CBD products. You can register to attend or view online and read all of the Board papers.
Katie PettiferChief Executive of FSA

Ein gwaith yn yr Asiantaeth Safonau Bwyd (ASB) yw sicrhau bod bwyd yn ddiogel ac yn ddilys. Yn y sector cig, mae hynny’n golygu cynnal arolygiadau cynhwysfawr mewn lladd-dai a busnesau prosesu cig. Mae’r gwaith hwn yn diogelu iechyd pobl ac anifeiliaid, yn cynorthwyo lles anifeiliaid, ac yn helpu i gynnal hyder mewn cig Prydeinig.

Yng nghyfarfod nesaf Bwrdd yr ASB, byddwn ni’n trafod dyfodol cymorth ariannol ar gyfer yr arolygiadau hyn ac yn ystyried argymhellion yn dilyn rhaglen sylweddol o ymgysylltu â’r diwydiant ac ymgynghoriad cyhoeddus diweddar.

Dros y ddwy flynedd ddiwethaf, rydyn ni wedi gweithio’n helaeth gyda busnesau, cyrff masnach a rhanddeiliaid eraill i ystyried sut y dylai gostyngiadau ar daliadau am arolygiadau cig, a ariennir gan drethdalwyr, weithredu yn y dyfodol.

Mae’r trefniadau presennol yn rhoi cymorth ariannol i fusnesau ar draws y sector, ond mae’r dystiolaeth sydd wedi’i chasglu drwy’r ymgynghoriad yn awgrymu y dylen ni dargedu’r cymorth yn fwy penodol at ladd-dai llai o faint, gan fod costau rheoleiddiol yn gallu bod yn fwy o faich iddyn nhw.

Yn aml, mae lladd-dai llai o faint yn chwarae rhan bwysig mewn economïau gwledig, gan roi cymorth i waith cynhyrchu bwyd lleol a darparu gwasanaethau y mae ffermwyr, cynhyrchwyr a defnyddwyr yn eu gwerthfawrogi.

Bwriad y cynigion y bydd Bwrdd yr ASB yn eu trafod yw sicrhau bod arian trethdalwyr yn cael ei ddefnyddio mewn ffordd sy’n cyflawni’r manteision ehangach hyn i’r system fwyd a’r economi, a hynny wrth barhau i gefnogi diogelwch bwyd a hyder defnyddwyr. Gallwch ddarllen rhagor am y cynigion hyn ym mhapur y Bwrdd sydd wedi’i gyhoeddi heddiw.

Mae taliadau am arolygiadau’n dal i fod yn bryder i lawer o fusnesau, ac rydyn ni’n deall y pwysau maen nhw’n eu hwynebu wrth i gostau cynyddu. Dyna pam mae’n bwysig bod penderfyniadau am gymorth yn y dyfodol yn cael eu llywio gan dystiolaeth, yn ogystal ag ymgynghoriadau parhaus â’r diwydiant a dealltwriaeth glir o’r effaith ehangach ar y sector.

Fel rheoleiddiwr tryloyw, rydyn ni am i’r rhai sydd â diddordeb yn y mater hwn gael y cyfle i glywed trafodaeth y Bwrdd yn uniongyrchol. Caiff cyfarfodydd ein Bwrdd eu cynnal yn gyhoeddus ac mae croeso i chi ddod yn bersonol neu ymuno o bell, fel y gallwch chi ddilyn y drafodaeth a chlywed ystyriaethau’r Bwrdd yn uniongyrchol.

Bydd y cyfarfod ddydd Mercher, 16 Medi, yn Abertawe. Mae’r agenda hefyd yn cynnwys ystod o faterion eraill sy’n bwysig i fwyd, gan gynnwys y rhaglen ‘Dyfodol Rheoleiddio Bwyd’, ein diweddariad gwyddoniaeth blynyddol, a materion mewn perthynas â rheoleiddio cynhyrchion CBD. Gallwch gofrestru i ddod i’r cyfarfod neu ei wylio ar-lein a darllen holl bapurau’r Bwrdd.
Katie PettiferPrif Weithredwr yr ASB

title: Interest in Higher Tier single-focus agreements

content.content: In July, we introduced a new Expression of Interest (EOI) process to widen participation in Countryside Stewardship Higher Tier (CSHT).
This made it possible for farmers and land managers to submit an EOI for:
We also introduced single-focus agreements, making it easier to apply for funding and focus on a particular environmental outcome. These support specific environmental priorities in:
To help us manage applications efficiently, we said that up to 1,200 single-focus agreements would be made available initially. To date, we’ve received over 650 EOIs for single-focus agreements.
This response reflects the appeal of a simpler approach that enables farmers and land managers to deliver meaningful environmental benefits through targeted, single-focus agreements.
While most EOIs received to date relate to species-rich grassland, we continue to welcome EOIs for scheduled monument management agreements.
These agreements can help secure the protection of important historic features while supporting appropriate land management.
The EOI process
Before submitting the online EOI form, you should:
After this, you can go ahead and complete the online EOI form on GOV.UK.
If you are interested in a single-focus agreement for species rich grassland and scheduled monument management, you will need to submit a separate EOI for each.

There is no automatic validation within the EOI form, so it is important that all details are entered accurately. Incorrect information, or insufficient permissions to act on behalf of a business, can delay progress or prevent an EOI from being taken forward.
Once you have submitted your EOI, you will be contacted within 10 weeks with information about the next steps.
Submitting an EOI does not automatically result in an agreement being offered, but it is the first step in the process and allows the relevant advisers to discuss the opportunity with you.

Natural England will continue to discuss species-rich grassland applications with interested applicants, while Historic England will contact those interested in scheduled monument management to discuss their proposals and any site visit requirements.
Looking ahead
We will continue to expand access to CSHT and keep farmers and land managers updated as further opportunities become available.
By subscribing to the Farming Blog, you'll be among the first to hear about future CSHT opportunities and other support available to farmers and land managers in England.

description: Interest in Countryside Stewardship Higher Tier (CSHT) single-focus agreements continues to grow, with 650 expressions of interest (EOIs) received since the offer opened at the end of July. This post covers the current areas of interest and how to submit an EOI.

title: Share your expertise and join our Scientific Advisory Committees
authors: Richard Smith – Member of the Science Council

content.content: Cymraeg
We are currently recruiting for new members to join our  Science Council and Scientific Advisory Committees (SACs).

Our committees are integral to the Food Standards Agency (FSA). They help us to be an effective science and evidence-led organisation. They help prioritise our work and ensure we provide accurate information to people.
The success of the SACs comes down to the members who are from a range of disciplines, enabling discussions and decisions to be made with diverse voices and a range of expertise.
To get a feel for what being a member of one of our SACs is like, we spoke to four current members to find out more.
Richard Smith – Member of the Science Council
Reverend Lesley A Stanley – Chair of the Committee on Toxicity of Chemicals in Food, Consumer Products and the Environment (COT)
Wendy Harwood – Member of the Advisory Committee on Novel Foods and Processes (ACNFP)
Barry Bradford – Associate member of the Advisory Committee on Animal Feedingstuffs (ACAF)
What is your role in the committee, and what are your responsibilities?

Richard Smith: I am a member, bringing expertise most specifically to the core FSA mission that “food is healthy” (the other 2 are that “food is safe” and “food is what it says it is”), as well as likely economic aspects (given my background) and experience in generating and using scientific evidence.

Reverend Lesley A Stanley: My role as Chair is to explain issues and articulate questions in a way that enables everybody to participate as we seek answers and formulate advice. Once we’ve reached an agreed view it’s my job to ensure that our advice is presented clearly in a form that will ensure its value to fellow experts, risk managers and consumers.
Wendy Harwood: My role in the committee is to contribute expertise in plant genetics, genetic technologies and other aspects of plant science.

Barry Bradford: My primary role involves using my knowledge and expertise in foodborne infectious diseases such as prion diseases to support the committee to perform risk assessments on animal feed additive applications. As a committee we also discuss and formulate position papers on broader issues relevant to its role.
What is it like working with the FSA?

Richard Smith: Enjoyable and rewarding. Like-minded colleagues, but from very different backgrounds, means there is always something to learn and very engaging debates to be had and all focused on a critical role to ensure that we can trust our food is safe and healthy.

Reverend Lesley A Stanley: What I love about working with the FSA is its collaborative, collegiate culture in which each contributor – expert, lay member or secretariat – plays to his or her strengths and everybody’s contribution is appreciated.

Wendy Harwood: Working with the FSA has been a very positive experience. I have worked with, and learnt a lot, from committee and FSA colleagues who cover a wide range of expertise. The committee provides an environment where members feel comfortable contributing to discussions and also asking questions when needed.

Barry Bradford: The FSA brings together diverse and experienced teams spanning academia, industry and administration all dedicated to the goal of making not only the food we eat safe but also the way we make it safer for all. These shared values permeate all levels of FSA work.
What is the best thing about being a member of your committee?
Richard Smith: Feeling that we are making a difference, protecting and improving the food that we eat through reviewing and promoting the scientific evidence base.

Reverend Lesley A Stanley: The joy of learning from good friends and colleagues as we address chemical risks that threaten the health and wellbeing of the UK population. Being part of a close-knit team in which everybody trusts each other and works together to do the best possible job for the FSA and the consumers it serves.

Wendy Harwood: The best thing is the great group of people I work with, for both the knowledge and support that they offer.  Also knowing that our work contributes to ensuring that food is safe for everyone is very rewarding.

Barry Bradford: Feeling very much a part of the FSA network. I have learned a lot from other committee members, both from their experience and approach. I feel both as a committee and individually we play a role in contributing to a One Health approach to food production and protecting consumer safety.
How has being a committee member helped you in your career?

Richard Smith: It has given me a different perspective on the food system and my own academic work and opened me up to a whole different network.  For those who have less experience in general of committees it is a great grounding and ‘toe in the water’ for these sorts of roles.

Reverend Lesley A Stanley: It’s widened my professional network, given me the opportunity to broaden and deepen my understanding of toxicology and allowed me to gain experience of risk assessment and risk management. It’s taught me numerous transferable skills, including the ability to quickly assimilate and evaluate large quantities of information and provide in-depth analysis and strategic guidance.

Wendy Harwood: Learning from committee members with very different expertise to my own has helped gain a broader perspective of how my work fits in. I have also gained a lot of committee experience which has been useful in other roles.

Barry Bradford: I have learned a lot in a short space of time working on the science advisory committee. From knowledge in unfamiliar fields of research and industrial practices to analytical and communication skills. FSA work provides first-hand insight into how scientific data is assessed and advises government policy.
Who would you encourage to apply?

Richard Smith: Anyone and everyone! If you are passionate about the safety, quality and healthiness of the food we eat, have experience in the use of scientific evidence, and enjoys working with others from very different perspectives this is a brilliant role.

Reverend Lesley A Stanley: Anybody who relishes the intellectual challenge of using their scientific expertise to serve consumers and the general public, who’s looking for the opportunity to be at the cutting edge of new advances as – or even before – they happen or who wants to join a welcoming and supportive professional network.

Wendy Harwood: I would encourage anyone who has relevant expertise and who is happy to contribute their thoughts to discussions both in person and online to apply. It helps to be able to explain complex science from your area in an accessible way.
Barry Bradford: I would encourage anyone that is truly passionate about the safety of food production and the food we eat to apply.

Joining an FSA Scientific Advisory Committee is an opportunity to use your expertise to make a real difference for consumers and the wider public. You'll engage with complex and emerging scientific issues, collaborate with experts from different backgrounds, and help ensure our advice is grounded in robust evidence. Find out more about the available roles and submit your application today.
Ar hyn o bryd, rydym yn recriwtio aelodau newydd ar gyfer ein Cyngor Gwyddoniaeth a’n Pwyllgorau Cynghori Gwyddonol.

Mae ein pwyllgorau’n rhan annatod o’r Asiantaeth Safonau Bwyd (ASB). Maen nhw’n ein helpu i fod yn sefydliad effeithiol sy’n cael ei arwain gan wyddoniaeth a thystiolaeth. Maen nhw’n ein helpu i flaenoriaethu ein gwaith ac i sicrhau ein bod ni’n rhoi gwybodaeth gywir i bobl.

Mae’r Pwyllgorau Cynghori Gwyddonol wedi bod yn llwyddiant, diolch i’w haelodau sy’n dod o ystod o ddisgyblaethau. Mae hyn yn golygu bod lleisiau amrywiol ac ystod o arbenigedd yn cael eu cynnwys wrth gynnal trafodaethau a gwneud penderfyniadau.
I gael syniad sut beth yw bod yn aelod o un o’n pwyllgorau, gwnaethon ni siarad â phedwar o’r aelodau presennol i gael gwybod mwy.
Richard Smith – Aelod o’r Cyngor Gwyddoniaeth
Y Parchedig Lesley A Stanley – Cadeirydd y Pwyllgor ar Wenwyndra Cemegion mewn Bwyd, Cynhyrchion Defnyddwyr a’r Amgylchedd (COT)
Wendy Harwood – Aelod o’r Pwyllgor Cynghori ar Fwydydd a Phrosesau Newydd (ACNFP)
Barry Bradford – Aelod cyswllt o’r Pwyllgor Cynghori ar Fwyd Anifeiliaid (ACAF)
Beth yw eich rôl ar y pwyllgor, a beth yw eich cyfrifoldebau?

Richard Smith: Aelod ydw i, ac rwy’n dod â’m harbenigedd i un o dair cenhadaeth graidd yr ASB yn benodol, sef bod “bwyd yn iach”. (Y ddwy arall yw bod “bwyd yn ddiogel” a’i fod yn “cyd-fynd â hyn sydd ar y label”.) Rwy hefyd yn cyfrannu at agweddau economaidd tebygol (o ystyried fy nghefndir a phrofiad o gynhyrchu a defnyddio tystiolaeth wyddonol).

Y Parchedig Lesley A Stanley: Fel Cadeirydd, fy rôl yw egluro materion a mynegi cwestiynau mewn ffordd sy’n galluogi pawb i gymryd rhan wrth i ni geisio atebion a llunio cyngor. Unwaith y byddwn ni wedi cytuno ar safbwynt, fy swydd i yw sicrhau bod ein cyngor yn cael ei gyflwyno’n glir ar ffurf a fydd yn sicrhau ei fod yn werthfawr i gyd-arbenigwyr, rheolwyr risg, a defnyddwyr.
Wendy Harwood: Fy rôl i yn y pwyllgor yw cyfrannu arbenigedd mewn geneteg planhigion, technolegau genetig, ac agweddau eraill ar wyddor planhigion.

Barry Bradford: Prif ddiben fy rôl yw defnyddio fy ngwybodaeth a’m harbenigedd mewn clefydau heintus a gludir gan fwyd, fel clefydau prion, i gefnogi’r pwyllgor i gynnal asesiadau risg ar geisiadau ar gyfer ychwanegion bwyd anifeiliaid. Fel pwyllgor, rydyn ni hefyd yn trafod ac yn llunio papurau safbwynt ar faterion ehangach sy’n berthnasol i’r pwyllgor.
Sut brofiad yw gweithio gyda’r ASB?

Richard Smith: Rwy’n ei fwynhau, ac mae’n rhoi boddhad i mi. Mae cydweithio â phobl sydd o’r un anian, ond o gefndiroedd gwahanol iawn, yn golygu bod rhywbeth i’w ddysgu bob amser a bod trafodaethau diddorol iawn i’w cael. Mae pawb yn canolbwyntio ar y rôl hanfodol sydd gennym ni i sicrhau y gallwn ymddiried bod ein bwyd yn ddiogel ac yn iach.

Y Parchedig Lesley A Stanley: Beth dw i’n dwlu arno am weithio gyda’r ASB yw ei diwylliant cydweithredol, colegol lle mae pawb sy’n cyfrannu – arbenigwyr, aelodau lleyg, a’r ysgrifenyddiaeth – yn manteisio ar eu cryfderau eu hunain, a lle mae cyfraniadau pawb yn cael eu gwerthfawrogi.

Wendy Harwood: Mae gweithio gyda’r ASB wedi bod yn brofiad cadarnhaol iawn. Rwy wedi dysgu llawer wrth weithio gydag aelodau eraill y pwyllgor a staff yr ASB, gan fod pawb yn gweithio ar draws ystod eang o feysydd. Mae’r pwyllgor yn darparu amgylchedd lle mae aelodau’n teimlo’n gyfforddus i gyfrannu at drafodaethau a hefyd i ofyn cwestiynau pan fo angen.

Barry Bradford: Mae’r ASB yn dwyn ynghyd dimau amrywiol a phrofiadol sy’n cwmpasu’r byd academaidd, y diwydiant a gweinyddiaeth, a phob un wedi’i ymrwymo i’r nod o sicrhau nid yn unig bod y bwyd rydyn ni’n ei fwyta’n ddiogel ond hefyd bod y ffordd rydyn ni’n ei wneud yn fwy diogel i bawb. Mae’r gwerthoedd cyffredin hyn yn treiddio i bob lefel o waith yr ASB.
Beth yw’r peth gorau am fod yn aelod o’ch pwyllgor chi?
Richard Smith: Teimlo ein bod ni’n gwneud gwahaniaeth, yn diogelu ac yn gwella’r bwyd rydyn ni’n ei fwyta drwy adolygu a hyrwyddo’r sail dystiolaeth wyddonol.

Y Parchedig Lesley A Stanley: Y llawenydd o ddysgu gan gydweithwyr a ffrindiau da, wrth i ni fynd i’r afael â’r risgiau cemegol sy’n bygwth iechyd a lles poblogaeth y DU. Bod yn rhan o dîm agos lle mae pawb yn ymddiried yn ei gilydd ac yn cydweithio i wneud y gwaith gorau posib i’r ASB a’r defnyddwyr y mae’n eu gwasanaethu.

Wendy Harwood: Y peth gorau yw’r grŵp gwych o bobl rwy’n gweithio gyda nhw, oherwydd yr wybodaeth a’r gefnogaeth maen nhw’n eu cynnig. Hefyd, mae gwybod bod ein gwaith yn cyfrannu at sicrhau bod bwyd yn ddiogel i bawb yn werthfawr iawn.

Barry Bradford: Teimlo’n rhan fawr o rwydwaith yr ASB. Dw i wedi dysgu llawer gan aelodau eraill y pwyllgor, drwy eu profiad neu eu dulliau o weithredu. Dw i’n teimlo ein bod ni, fel pwyllgor ac yn unigol, yn chwarae rhan wrth gyfrannu at ddull ‘Iechyd Cyfunol’ o gynhyrchu bwyd a diogelu defnyddwyr.
Sut mae bod yn aelod pwyllgor wedi eich helpu yn eich gyrfa?

Richard Smith: Mae wedi rhoi persbectif gwahanol i mi ar y system fwyd ac ar fy ngwaith academaidd fy hun, ac mae wedi rhoi cyfle i mi ymuno â rhwydwaith hollol wahanol. I’r rhai sydd â llai o brofiad yn gyffredinol o bwyllgorau, mae’n sail wych sy’n galluogi rhywun i ‘brofi’r dyfroedd’ yn y mathau hyn o rolau.

Y Parchedig Lesley A Stanley: Mae wedi ehangu fy rhwydwaith proffesiynol, wedi rhoi’r cyfle i mi ehangu a dyfnhau fy nealltwriaeth o docsicoleg, ac wedi fy ngalluogi i ennill profiad o asesu a rheoli risgiau. Mae wedi dysgu nifer o sgiliau trosglwyddadwy i mi, gan gynnwys y gallu i gymathu a gwerthuso symiau mawr o wybodaeth yn gyflym a darparu dadansoddiad manwl ac arweiniad strategol.

Wendy Harwood: Mae dysgu gan aelodau’r pwyllgor sydd ag arbenigedd gwahanol iawn i’m harbenigedd fy hun wedi fy helpu i gael persbectif ehangach o sut mae fy ngwaith yn cyfrannu. Rwy hefyd wedi ennill llawer o brofiad o bwyllgora sydd wedi bod yn ddefnyddiol mewn rolau eraill.

Barry Bradford: Dw i wedi dysgu llawer mewn cyfnod byr o weithio ar y pwyllgor cynghori gwyddonol – o wybodaeth mewn meysydd ymchwil anghyfarwydd ac arferion y diwydiant, i sgiliau dadansoddi a chyfathrebu. Mae gwaith yr ASB yn rhoi mewnwelediad uniongyrchol i sut mae data gwyddonol yn cael ei asesu a sut mae’n llywio polisi’r llywodraeth.
Pwy fyddech chi’n ei annog i wneud cais?

Richard Smith: Pawb! Os ydych chi’n angerddol am sicrhau bod y bwyd rydyn ni’n ei fwyta’n ddiogel, yn iach a’i fod o ansawdd uchel, os oes gennych chi brofiad o ddefnyddio tystiolaeth wyddonol, ac os ydych chi’n mwynhau gweithio gyda phobl eraill sydd â safbwyntiau gwahanol iawn, dyma rôl wych i chi.

Y Parchedig Lesley A Stanley: Unrhyw un sy’n mwynhau’r her ddeallusol o ddefnyddio arbenigedd gwyddonol i wasanaethu defnyddwyr a’r cyhoedd, sy’n chwilio am y cyfle i fod ar flaen y gad o ran datblygiadau newydd wrth iddyn nhw ddigwydd – neu hyd yn oed cyn iddyn nhw ddigwydd – neu sydd eisiau ymuno â rhwydwaith proffesiynol croesawgar a chefnogol.

Wendy Harwood: Byddwn i’n annog pawb i wneud cais os oes ganddyn nhw’r arbenigedd perthnasol a’u bod yn hapus i gyfrannu eu syniadau at drafodaethau wyneb yn wyneb ac ar-lein. Mae’n helpu os ydych chi’n gallu esbonio gwyddoniaeth gymhleth o’ch maes mewn ffordd syml.
Barry Bradford: Byddwn i’n annog unrhyw un sydd wir yn angerddol am ddiogelwch y broses gynhyrchu bwyd, a diogelwch y bwyd rydyn ni’n ei fwyta, i wneud cais.

Mae ymuno ag un o Bwyllgorau Cynghori Gwyddonol yr ASB yn gyfle i ddefnyddio eich arbenigedd i wneud gwahaniaeth gwirioneddol i ddefnyddwyr a’r cyhoedd yn ehangach. Byddwch chi’n ymdrin â materion gwyddonol cymhleth sy’n dod i’r amlwg, yn cydweithio ag arbenigwyr o wahanol gefndiroedd, ac yn helpu i sicrhau bod ein cyngor wedi’i seilio ar dystiolaeth gadarn. Dysgwch fwy am y rolau sydd ar gael a chyflwynwch eich cais heddiw.

title: From sustainability champions to sustainability by design – Part Two

content.content: Thinking about sustainability earlier
Some of the biggest opportunities to improve sustainability arise long before a service enters operation.
Decisions made during concept development, architecture design and service planning can influence environmental performance, operational efficiency, and costs for many years to come.

For this reason, I believe sustainability should increasingly be viewed as a non-functional requirement, sitting alongside established considerations such as security, reliability, availability, accessibility, and safety.

Practical examples can be surprisingly simple. They might include designing software to use resources more efficiently, optimising cloud consumption, managing data throughout its lifecycle, avoiding unnecessary duplication of infrastructure, extending asset life where appropriate and applying circular economy principles.
These decisions often deliver benefits that extend beyond environmental outcomes, improving efficiency and reducing costs at the same time.
The opportunity in procurement and delivery
In my experience, some of the greatest opportunities to improve sustainability come through procurement and delivery activities.
Sustainability is often considered during supplier selection, but its real value can be realised when those considerations continue throughout contract delivery and service operation.

Programme teams, project managers, service managers, and commercial specialists all influence decisions that shape outcomes. Routine supplier reviews, governance meetings, risk discussions, and performance assessments provide natural opportunities to consider sustainability alongside cost, schedule, risk, and service performance.

Where sustainability commitments have been made during procurement, these should continue to be monitored throughout delivery. Equally, where sustainability information is available, it should become part of normal management conversations rather than being treated as a separate reporting stream.
Balancing ambition with practicality
Another lesson from experience is that sustainability measures need to be proportionate, evidence-based, and financially viable.
Environmental improvement remains important, but organisations must also consider operational effectiveness, resilience, affordability, and deliverability.

The objective should not be sustainability at any cost. Instead, it should be achieving the greatest overall benefit through solutions that are practical, affordable, and capable of long-term adoption.
Often, the most successful initiatives are not the most ambitious. They are the ones that can be adopted consistently and sustained over time.
Sustainability and resilience go hand in hand
One observation that has become increasingly clear is that sustainability and resilience are often closely connected.

Many sustainable ICT practices can also improve efficiency, reduce operating costs, make better use of resources, and strengthen long-term affordability. They can help organisations get more value from existing assets while reducing dependencies and avoiding unnecessary waste.
Viewed through this lens, sustainability is not simply an environmental objective. It becomes part of delivering digital services that are resilient, supportable, and fit for the future.
As organisations continue to focus on resilience, efficiency, and long-term value, I believe this relationship will become increasingly important.
Looking ahead
The challenge facing digital organisations today is no longer whether sustainability should be considered. The challenge is how we make it part of everyday decision-making.
My experience suggests that the answer lies in integration rather than additional process.

By embedding sustainability within existing governance, commercial, delivery, and assurance arrangements, we can move away from treating it as a separate activity and make it a natural part of delivering digital capability.

Ultimately, success will depend on making sustainability business as usual — not something we do in addition to delivering digital services, but something that is built into the way those services are designed, acquired, delivered, and operated from the outset.

Christopher Gale is an Acquisition Safety and Environmental Manager, Digital & Data, at the Ministry of Defence.
